passage: In the May heat wave the power went out in the Nagpur flat for four hours a day, and Eshaan wanted to cool his room without a fan. He didn't hunt for a design. He asked: how does heat leave a warm thing? By touching something cooler, by moving air, or by water turning into vapour, which carries heat off with it. The last one he could do with what they had. 'Sweat does that for us,' he told Aditi, his sister. He hung a damp cotton sheet across the window so the breeze crossed it, and set a shallow tray of water beneath. After half an hour the room felt a little cooler, though the air felt damp. He wrote: works, needs wind, cloth needs re-wetting.

"Why are you soaking a towel?" Neelam asked, watching her sister Arohi at the balcony.
"I'm making a cooler for my room. The fan just blows hot air."
"Buy one."
"No. First question," Arohi said, wringing the towel. "How does my body cool down?"
"Sweat?"
"Right. Sweat dries, and drying takes heat away from the skin. So what I need isn't cold air from a machine. I need water drying in front of the fan."
"So you're sweating for the room."
Arohi laughed. "Kind of. Wet cloth in front of the fan, air goes through, water dries, air comes out cooler." She draped the towel over a plastic crate in front of the table fan and switched it on.
Neelam stood in front of it. "Oh. That's actually cooler."
"Now I need to keep the cloth wet. Maybe a bottle dripping on top."

qa.a: She draped the towel over a plastic crate in front of the table fan.

qa.q: How can you tell Arohi felt confident about her idea?
qa.a: She laughed at Neelam's joke and kept explaining calmly, sure that water drying would cool the air.

qa.q: What else could Arohi test to improve the cooler, and why?
qa.a: She could try a thinner cloth or a wider crate, since more air passing over wet cloth may cool better.

qa.q: How does Neelam see Arohi's plan?
qa.a: Neelam is doubtful at first and suggests buying one, then is surprised and impressed when the air feels cooler.

passage:
I'm Shalini, and last May our room at the top of the building was like an oven. We couldn't afford a cooler, and the ones in the shop were big metal boxes with pumps.
My friend Nilesh said, "Just watch a video and copy one."
But I didn't want to copy a box. I wanted to understand. So I asked myself: when I come out of a swimming pool, why do I feel cold even in summer? Because the water on my skin is drying, and drying pulls heat away.
So all I needed was water drying where the air was moving. I hung a wet cotton dupatta across the window, where the evening breeze came in, and put a bucket below so it could drip.
The room dropped from unbearable to okay. Not a miracle. But I understood why it worked, and I could fix it when it dried out.

qa.q: What did Shalini hang across the window?
qa.a: Shalini hung a wet cotton dupatta across the window.

qa.q: How did Shalini feel about the result?
qa.a: Shalini felt satisfied and a bit proud, not because it was a miracle but because understanding why it worked made it easy to fix.

qa.q: What else could Shalini try to make the cooling last longer?
qa.a: Shalini could set up a slow drip to keep the dupatta wet, since drying out is when the cooling stops.

qa.q: How might Nilesh see Shalini's approach?
qa.a: Nilesh suggested copying a video, so Nilesh may be surprised that thinking it through from basics worked without buying anything.

grounding: It shows a teenager asking how heat leaves a body and using a damp cloth for evaporation rather than copying a shop-bought cooler.
